Welcome
I am delighted to welcome you to the Stone Bay School website. I hope you will find the information here gives you a flavour of our very special school.
We specialise in providing both day and residential education for pupils aged 4 to 19 years who have a diagnosis of ASD, along with severe and complex learning needs. We currently provide for 112 pupils.
Our school is situated on Stone Bay in Broadstairs in a beautiful Victorian building overlooking the sea. The local coastal environment provides many unique and enjoyable learning opportunities for our pupils.

Leading Parent Partnership
Stone Bay proudly achieved the Leading Parent Partnership Award in November 2024
Leading Parent Partnership Award (LPPA) is a nationally recognised award that helps schools to work in partnership with all parents and carers. The award hopes to increase parental participation in school life, which could help to improve pupils' progress, punctuality, attendance and behaviour, ultimately leading to improved outcomes in all aspects of school life.
We like to involve you from the very start of your child’s journey at Stone Bay!
Going forward, Stone Bay is committed to building on its success and will continue to listen to and involve parents at all stages of their child's journey through our school.
At Stone Bay, we believe that a strong partnership between our school and families is essential to the success and well-being of our students. We are deeply committed to regularly seeking your opinions, listening to your concerns, and responding to your feedback.
We recognise that your insights are invaluable, and together, we can continue to create an environment where every child can thrive. Whether through surveys, meetings, or informal conversations, we encourage and welcome your thoughts, suggestions, and any areas where you feel we can improve.
Thank you for your continued support and collaboration. We look forward to working together to ensure the best possible experience for your child at Stone Bay.

Stone Bay Achieves Silver UNICEF RSSA AWARD
Stone Bay School receives prestigious UNICEF UK Award
Stone Bay School has been awarded the Silver Rights Respecting School Award by UNICEF UK.
UNICEF is the world’s leading organisation working for children and their rights. The Rights Respecting Schools Award is granted to schools that show commitment to promoting and realising children’s rights and encouraging adults, children, and young people to respect the rights of others in school. Silver is given to schools that make excellent progress towards embedding the principles of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child into its ethos and curriculum. There are over 1,300 schools across England, Scotland, Northern Ireland, and Wales that have achieved Silver and over 600 schools that have been awarded Gold, the next step up and highest accolade granted by UNICEF UK.

Personal Development
Personal Development
At Stone Bay School, Personal Development is at the heart of our vision of
“Getting it right for every pupil.”
We are committed to supporting the whole child —academically, socially, emotionally and personally— within a safe, caring and inclusive community where every pupil is respected and valued.
Guided by our core values of Evolving Excellence, Trust, Empowerment, Fairness and Collaboration, we recognise that every pupil is unique.
As a UNICEF Silver Rights Respecting School, children’s rights, dignity and participation are embedded in our ethos, promoting wellbeing and enabling pupils to develop confidence, resilience and independence.
We place a strong emphasis on Preparation for Adulthood, equipping pupils with the life skills, independence and self-belief they need for their next steps.
Pupils benefit from opportunities that promote diversity and inclusion, outdoor learning, creative expression, physical activity and enrichment beyond the classroom.
Communication is supported through personalised approaches, ensuring every pupil can express themselves and engage meaningfully with others.
Through Pupil Voice, we empower learners to be active participants in school life, ensuring they feel listened to, respected and valued.
Our range of Therapeutic Offers is designed to meet the diverse and complex needs of our pupils, providing targeted support that helps remove barriers to learning and wellbeing.
Our Personal Development provision includes a carefully planned, year-long programme of experience that supports pupil wellbeing, positive relationships and a strong sense of belonging.

Zoolab visits Stone Bay 2026
Zoolab recently visited Stone Bay School and brought along some fascinating animals for our pupils to meet. The children had the opportunity to see and learn about a range of creatures, including a snake, a tarantula and even a cockroach!
Many pupils were excited to get involved and enjoyed the chance to stroke or carefully handle the animals, with plenty of smiles and brave moments throughout the sessions. Just as importantly, some pupils were able to communicate that they preferred not to touch the animals, which was equally respected and celebrated. Being able to express their feelings and make choices is an important part of developing confidence and self-advocacy.
It was a fantastic experience for everyone and a great opportunity for pupils to learn about animals in a fun and engaging way! 🐛🪳

Rufus the guide dog visits stone bay
Pupils at Stone Bay School were recently inspired by a visit from Aaron and his guide dog, Rufus. Aaron spoke to pupils about what it means to live with visual impairment and how guide dogs help people navigate the world safely and independently.
During the visit, pupils had the opportunity to meet Rufus and learn about the important training guide dogs receive. Aaron explained how Rufus helps him in everyday life and answered pupils’ thoughtful questions about the partnership between a guide dog and its owner.
The visit was both engaging and educational, helping pupils better understand how guide dogs support people with sight loss. Inspired by Aaron and Rufus, the school is now hoping to sponsor a Guide Dogs puppy, allowing pupils to follow the puppy’s journey as it trains to become a future guide dog. 🐕‍🦺
Stone Bay School would like to thank Aaron and Rufus for such an inspiring and memorable visit.

Governors
The role of the school governor and governing bodies:
The role of the school governor is demanding but very rewarding and is an excellent way to give back to your local community. School governing bodies are responsible for working with the school to ensure that it delivers a good quality education. Together with the headteacher, who is responsible for day-to-day management, they set the school’s aims and policies.
Role of School Governor
Key roles of governors:
They also carry out a number of other important duties, which include:
If you are interested in serving as a Stone Bay School governor please don’t hesitate to contact us. We particularly welcome applications from existing parents.
Determining how the school’s budget is spent.
The appointment and dismissal of staff.
Hearing appeals and grievances.
Setting standards for pupils’ behaviour and discipline.
Our Current Governing Body:
The Governing Body of Stone Bay School reconstituted on 11 July 2023 in line with the School Governance (Constitution) (England) Regulations 2012. Twelve governors are appointed to sit on the school’s governing board. They review the governance structure, terms of reference and standing orders on an annual basis, and have adopted the ‘circle’ structure, which requires the governing body to convene at least six times per year, and for governors to carry out regular monitoring responsibilities and report back to the full governing body.

Positive Wellbeing for Children and Families
Research consistently shows a strong link between positive well-being, robust mental health, and the ability to build resilience, all of which lead directly to improved outcomes for both children and adults.
The NHS have used research based evidence to highlight 5 steps that we can all take to improve our mental health and wellbeing:
You can find out more about the 5 Steps to Mental Wellbeing here.
We have put together the information below to explore how these five steps can be implemented both at home and at school to effectively support and improve mental health and well-being for neurodivergent children and their families.
Connect with other people.
Be physically active.
Learn new skills.
Give to others (acts of kindness).
Pay attention to the present moment (mindfulness).
The 5 Steps to Mental Wellbeing for Neurodivergent Children & Their Families
These steps are designed to be simple, predictable, and supportive for both the child and the parent/carer.
This step focusses on meaningful, low-stress interactions rather than overwhelming social demands.
For the Parent/Carer
* Shared Special Interest: Spend time with family doing an activity you love, like watching a favourite show or building with blocks. This is a calm way to be together.
* Follow the Child's Lead: Join their special interest (e.g., talk about trains, play a video game) for 10 minutes without asking lots of questions.
* Predictable Greetings: Use a familiar way to say hello or goodbye (a high-five, a wave, or a specific phrase) to reduce anxiety.
* Use Visuals: Use visual schedules or social stories to prepare the child for visitors or social calls.
* Check-In Spot: Identify a quiet, safe person or spot to go to when you feel lonely or worried.
* Connect with Others: Reach out to other parents of neurodivergent children for understanding and support. You are not alone.
Focus on sensory-regulating and predictable movements that help discharge energy and calm the nervous system.
For the Parent/Carer
* Sensory Movement: Try activities that help you feel organised, like swinging, deep pressure squeezes (a 'squish'), or bouncing on a gym ball.
* Schedule Movement Breaks: Build 3-5 short 'Movement Breaks' into the daily visual schedule (e.g., 5 minutes of jumping jacks, a walk around the garden).
* Predictable Routes: Take a walk on the same route every day so you know exactly what to expect.
* Create a Safe Space: Ensure a safe area for stimming (self-stimulating behaviour) and intense movement, like a trampoline or a cushioned corner.
* Heavy Work: Help with a chore that involves 'heavy work' (pushing a laundry basket, carrying heavy books) to feel grounded.
* Reward Effort, Not Perfection: Praise them for trying, even if they only move for a short time.
This step is about tuning into the immediate environment for specific details that provide comfort and understanding, rather than abstract "mindfulness."
For the Parent/Carer
* Sensory Focus: Notice a specific, comfortable sensory detail: the colour of a favourite toy, the sound of the dishwasher, or the texture of a soft blanket.
* Use Concrete Language: Guide them to "Take Notice" using very clear, concrete questions: "What is the temperature of the water?" or "Can you hear the clock ticking?"
* Routine Check: Look at your visual schedule to know what is happening now and what is next. This helps you feel in control.
* Slow Down Transition: Pause before moving to the next activity. Give a 5-minute warning and a clear cue.
* Comfort Spot: Spend a quiet moment in your safe space with your favourite items, focusing on how they feel and smell.
* Model Calm: Take a deep breath yourself and describe what you are noticing (e.g., "I notice the soft light outside").
Focus on mastering specific, functional skills and learning new ways to self-regulate and manage emotions.
For the Parent/Carer
* Master a Skill: Practise a specific, useful life skill (tying shoes, making a snack) until you feel confident.
* Break It Down: Use task analysis (breaking a skill into small steps) and visuals to teach new routines and skills.
* Learn a Tool: Practise using a tool to manage big feelings, like a fidget toy or a simple breathing technique (e.g., 'Bumblebee Breath').
* Focus on Strengths: Create opportunities for the child to use their special interest or natural talent to achieve something and feel successful.
* Understand Feelings: Learn to name your feelings using emotions cards or a feelings chart.
* Teach Self-Advocacy: Help your child learn one phrase they can use to ask for help or a break (e.g., "I need quiet").
This is about finding structured, predictable, and low-pressure ways to contribute, which builds self-esteem and a sense of belonging.
For the Parent/Carer
* Fixed Task: Complete your one specific chore on the schedule (e.g., feed the pet, wipe the table). Knowing your job helps you feel important.
* Structure the Giving: Assign one clear, consistent job to the child each day/week, making the expectations totally predictable.
* Help a Friend/Family: Offer help in a simple, non-verbal way, like handing someone a needed item or sharing a favourite toy.
* Acknowledge Their Contribution: Use specific praise: "Thank you for putting the cups away! You were so helpful."
* Share a Special Interest: Teach a family member one fun fact about your special interest.
* Connect Giving to Routine: Integrate the 'giving' activity into a familiar daily routine so it becomes expected and less stressful.

pageCache.text:
Forest's Fundraiser for Little Princess Trust
We’re so proud of our pupil, Forest, who is taking on the amazing challenge of cutting his long hair to raise money for the Little Princess Trust. If you’d like to support him, please see the donation details below.
Forest, an 11-year-old boy who attends Stone Bay School, has made an incredible decision to donate his long, luscious locks to The Little Princess Trust, a charity that provides real hair wigs to children who have lost their hair due to cancer treatments or conditions like Alopecia.
Diagnosed with autism and global developmental delay at the age of three, Forest has always faced challenges, particularly when it comes to sensory overload. For years, haircuts were an overwhelming experience. However, everything changed when Forest learned about a charity that makes wigs for children with cancer, relying on generous people like him to donate their own hair.
Inspired by this, Forest made the heartfelt decision to part with his hair in the hopes of making another child feel better. "I want to help," Forest said, expressing his wish to give back to those in need.
The Little Princess Trust, which provides wigs free of charge to young cancer patients, is also one of the largest funders of childhood cancer research in the UK. The charity’s work relies entirely on donations from kind-hearted individuals like Forest and others in the community.
Forest’s selfless act of generosity is a reminder that even small actions can make a big difference. He hopes that his donation will bring comfort to another child and inspire others to consider doing the same.

pageCache.text:
World Book Day 2026
On Thursday, Stone Bay stepped into a world of books, fun and imagination as we celebrated World Book Day. Our pupils — and some members of staff — arrived dressed as their favourite book characters, bringing stories to life around the school. Miss Trunchbull, Harry Potter, Willy Wonka, The Cat in the Hat and many other wonderful characters could be spotted taking part in the Daily Mile.
Each class chose a book to explore and created fantastic story sacks, which will now be kept in our library for everyone to enjoy. Throughout the day, pupils experienced stories in a variety of engaging ways, including sensory play, story massage and DEAR (Drop Everything and Read) time.
In the afternoon, pupils were delighted to share a range of exciting activities with their parents. It was a truly wonderful day, with reading for pleasure at the heart of everything we did.

pageCache.pageTitle: Stone Bay School - Rich Rhythms Drumming Workshop
pageCache.text:
Rich Rhythms Drumming Workshop
Rich Rhythms brought energy, excitement, and plenty of noise to our school this week with an unforgettable drumming workshop for pupils across all year groups.
Children had the opportunity to explore rhythm, teamwork, and creativity through a series of interactive sessions led by the talented Rich Rhythms team. From learning basic beats to performing together as a group, pupils were fully engaged and thoroughly enjoyed the hands-on experience.
The workshop not only introduced students to the joy of music and percussion but also helped build confidence, listening skills, and collaboration. The sound of drums echoed through the school as children embraced the chance to express themselves in a fun and unique way.
It was a fantastic experience for everyone involved, and we would like to thank Rich Rhythms for delivering such an inspiring and memorable day.

Victorian day
On Wednesday 15th July, we stepped back in time and designed a fantastic Victorian Day full of activities, games, music, food and plenty of laughter.
The pupils enjoyed watching a traditional Punch and Judy show, chatting with our wonderful Dickens characters who kindly gave up their time to visit the school, and taking part in a range of Victorian sports and games.
Everyone enjoyed a picnic in the sunshine and had the opportunity to capture memories in our Victorian-themed photo booth. The day was filled with smiles, excitement and lots of opportunities for pupils to experience what life might have been like during the Victorian era.
To finish the day, we all enjoyed singing alongside Hannah, performing songs from Oliver and celebrating together through music.
It was a huge success, and we are already looking forward to seeing how we can make next year’s event even bigger and better!
